Subject: Private endpoint egress — requirements and evidence request

Logan / team,

Thanks again for the walkthrough yesterday. NovaCorp is preparing our firewall/edge rules for the Redwood private endpoint and we need to lock down egress origination and documentation before our security sign-off. High-level asks from our side:

- Guidance on allowed egress modes: static NAT vs ephemeral NAT vs customer-managed proxy.
- Clarification on whether TLS inspection (SNI/DNS) is required on our edge or if mTLS between our proxy and Redwood is supported.

Subject: Re: Private endpoint egress — requirements and evidence request

Rachel — thanks, great notes. I annotated the attached CSV with our suggested egress mapping and wrote up an operational summary below. High-level options (tradeoffs):

1) Dedicated static egress pool (recommended for strict allowlists)
   - Redwood reserves N static IPv4 addresses per region and binds customer traffic to those addresses via NAT egress pools.
   - Pros: single CIDR to allow, simple firewall rules, no need for DNS split-horizon.
   - Cons: subscription add-on, modest monthly fee.

2) Ephemeral NAT + IP escrow evidence (acceptable for many customers)
   - Ephemeral NAT with predictable rotation windows; we provide an IP rotation schedule and signed attestations showing current allocations.
   - Pros: lower cost.
   - Cons: requires your firewall to accept a rotation window or use a short-lived proxy.

3) Customer-managed outbound proxy (most flexible)
   - Your proxy does mTLS to Redwood control-plane endpoints; Redwood accepts proxy-originated connections and attributes sessions to your tenant.
   - Pros: you keep egress ownership and local inspection.
   - Cons: requires additional configuration on your side (proxy certs, SNI passthrough if you need it).

Recommended firewall rules (minimum):
- Allow outbound TCP 443 to the Redwood control-plane FQDNs listed in the CSV.
- Open ports 5222 and 443 for telemetry/metrics where indicated. (We prefer 443 multiplexed).
- If you cannot inspect TLS, a static egress pool avoids the need for SNI-based rules.

IP/Port inventory (excerpt from attached CSV):
- 34.201.78.12/32 : control-plane-01.us.redwood.net : TCP 443
- 34.201.78.13/32 : control-plane-02.us.redwood.net : TCP 443
- 34.201.79.5/32  : artifacts-fetch.us.redwood.net : TCP 443

Operational notes:
- Static pool customers get a signed manifest (PDF) listing assigned IPs and the date-of-assignment for compliance artifact purposes.
- Ephemeral rotations happen every 7 days by default; we can shorten to 24 hours on request but will include a signed rotation log for audit.
- If you opt for a customer-managed proxy, we support mTLS with mutual certificate validation (we will exchange CA pins via a secure link).

Next steps:
- I attached egress-ip-inventory-20260910.csv with the full mapping.
- Please indicate which mode you prefer (Static / Ephemeral / Proxy) so Marissa and I can scope the artifact package and pricing.
- If useful, we can run a 30-minute VPC walk-through with your neteng team tomorrow morning.

Logan
Logan Wright
Principal Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Private endpoint egress — requirements and evidence request

Rachel — jumping in from compliance. A few clarifications that will help NovaCorp's SOC2 package: 

- If you choose the static egress pool we will provide: 
  * Signed IP assignment manifest (PDF) with certifying signature from Redwood Compliance.
  * A statement describing our IP rotation policy ("none" for static pool) and the escrow procedure.
  * A short operations-runbook describing how to validate the IPs during an audit (curl tests, TLS fingerprint).

- For ephemeral NAT customers we will include: 
  * Rotation logs (signed), window policy, and an automated webhook you can subscribe to for rotation events.
  * Guidance for firewall whitelisting during rotation windows (recommended: allow the ephemeral subnet and apply FQDN-based controls if your firewall supports it).

- On TLS inspection: Redwood supports mutual-TLS between your proxy and our control-plane. We do not require you to perform TLS deep inspection of payloads; SNI & DNS-based allowlists are an option but not required if you use a static pool or mTLS proxy.

Pricing note: static egress pool is an add-on. Logan will follow up with the exact SKU.

Please confirm which model you prefer so we can bundle the correct attestations and schedule the implementation window.

Thanks,
Marissa
Marissa Cole
Director, Customer Security & Trust, Redwood Inference
